properties.containerTitle: CSL's container-title — the journal, book or site the work appears in — stored in camel case because the Cypher dialect has no quoted identifiers; container-title itself cannot be written
properties.fetched: what answered the record, when, and from which identifier

properties.id: the work's identity, a UUID the shell mints; the node id is node:<id>
properties.kind: the CSL type of the work: article-journal, book, chapter, paper-conference, thesis, report, webpage, post, dataset, software or document

content.semantics: A work of the instance's bibliography — a bibliographic work, the cited thing — a root node with no parent and no block flag, so it is never offered among the kinds a document's block may take; its record in CSL-JSON shape, the shape a DOI resolves to, the engine exports and the citation processor consumes. Declared by bibliography under BO_0291; named work rather than source because node:source is already relations' relation type (user decision, 2026-09-23). The identifier — DOI, ISBN or URL — is the identity for duplicates. A citation is a run of a text block carrying cite with the work's identity and no text of its own, drawn as the work's number, which the document read derives and never stores. The record's two hyphenated CSL keys are stored as containerTitle and publisherPlace, the dialect having no quoted identifiers; the extension maps them at its write and its read.

conventions.citeByRun: A citation is a run of the sentence carrying cite: {work: <workId>, locator?} and empty text, proposed with propose_document_changes like any change to the sentence. Never write the number: the document's read derives it.
conventions.fetchDontDraft: A work that is not in the bibliography is fetched with fetch_record — its DOI, ISBN, PMID, arXiv id or an address — and proposed with propose_work. Never draft a record from memory: a wrong author or year in a reference is worse than no reference.
conventions.locatorWhenItHelps: Give a locator — p. 12, §3, fig. 2 — when the claim rests on one place in a long work; leave it out otherwise.
conventions.oneWorkOnce: propose_work refuses a work the bibliography already holds and names it: cite that one.
conventions.readBeforeCiting: Read the bibliography with read_works before citing, and cite by the workId it answers. A work cited twice keeps its number.

content.goal: Cite what a claim rests on, from the instance's bibliography, where a reader would want to follow it; add a work to the bibliography only from a record you fetched.
content.outputContract: A conclusion naming the works you cited and any you proposed; zero or more works staged into the run's group; the sentences carrying their cite runs staged beside them.
content.permittedOperations: read_works to read the bibliography; fetch_record, the kernel's, to fetch a work's record; propose_work to stage a work into your group; propose_document_changes to stage a sentence carrying a cite run. Nothing you hold writes truth.
preconditions: The bibliography extension is active: read_works answers. If it does not, say so and cite nothing.
You can say which sentence the work supports; a citation stands where a claim does.

content.description: Propose a work to the instance's bibliography: the record fetch_record answered for it, as it came — one CSL-JSON item — and what you fetched it from. The work is staged into your proposal group, never written as truth: the person accepts it with the rest. A work sharing a DOI, an ISBN or an address with one the bibliography already holds is refused, naming that work: cite it instead. Fetch the record first; do not draft one from memory. Once proposed, cite it by the workId this answers.

conventions.atomicProposal: One extension change is one proposal group: every staged revision and relation belongs to the same group and is accepted or rejected as a unit. Never trickle per-file proposals; a half-applied extension state must never be materializable.
conventions.humanWritesCostAConfirmation: Every human-class write from the shell parks at the kernel bridge and waits for a confirmation on the kernel's own origin — no human mutation travels from the app origin to CCGW. Budget one cross-origin confirmation per write. That is proportionate for occasional truth like creating a channel and disproportionate for continuous editing, so a surface that writes on every keystroke needs a different shape than one that writes on a button.
conventions.oneOpenProposalPerBlock: A block carries at most one open proposal: every block type declares singleOpenCandidate, so a candidate of a block another open group already holds a candidate of is refused by the core — there is no second candidate to stage beside the first. Work bearing on such a block builds on the candidate that stands, staged into that group as a refinement (the document tools' refines; conventions.openProposals of ui.shell.documents), rather than opening a competing one, so the person answers once. Nothing here answers a proposal: accepting and rejecting stay the person's (proofsAreNotProposals). (BO_0271)
conventions.proofsAreNotProposals: Never stage a proposal whose intended outcome is rejection. A proof-only group is indistinguishable from a real one at the review surface — the rationale is rendered as ordinary text — so after a run of proposals that all deserved acceptance, one that did not will be accepted by the same motion. Construct demonstrations so the refusal is the whole proof and stop there: a refused mutation stages nothing and opens no group. Acceptance is the one non-delegable human action in the architecture and its entire value is the attention behind it, so anything that produces frequent near-identical almost-always-correct proposals is spending that attention down.
conventions.valuesTravelAsParameters:
How a statement says values, which the grammar will not let you guess:
- Every value beyond a scalar travels beside the statement in the tool call's parameters field, which is one JSON object written as text — for example parameters: "{\"bid\": \"art-x.b1\", \"runs\": [{\"text\": \"...\"}]}". The statement writes $name where a value belongs; lists and objects have no literal form inside the statement itself, and runs: [{text: ...}] inline is a parse error every time.
- Every $name in the statement must have a key in that JSON object. An empty parameters value beside a parameterized statement is always wrong, and resending a refused statement without filling it changes nothing.
- A script is one or more statements separated by semicolons; CREATE ... RELATE ... in one breath is a parse error at RELATE. Aliases scope per statement but parameters are request-global, so one parameters object serves the whole script: the canonical block write is CREATE (n:Text {id: $bid, runs: $runs, order: $order}); RELATE childRef -[r:CONTAINS]-> parentRef, with bid, runs, order, childRef and parentRef all keys of the one JSON object.
- RELATE endpoint refs resolve from parameters — <ref>NodeId first, then <ref> — and those values carry the node: prefix (childRef: "node:art-x.b1"), even though the id property inside CREATE content is bare. The ref names an existing node; the id property mints one.
- When syntax is uncertain, calliopa_explain compiles a statement without executing it. Explain and correct rather than retrying a refusal unchanged — the diagnostics name what they want.
conventions.whereRequirementsLive: An extension's requirements and open work live in its own docs/ members (docs/system/**/*.md under the live-line protocol), read through calliopa_query like its code. An extension's changes are its own docs/changes/ members (BO_0254): docs/changes/<PREFIX>_NNNN_TYPE_<short-name>.md in its subtree, finished ones under docs/changes/completed/, each carrying its status in a Status: line from idea, draft, ready, wip, completed, rejected. They are written and revised the way every other docs member is — from a checkout, in the proposal that carries the code — and rendered read-only in the shell's Extensions section. A run working from the composer holds no checkout and so writes none. A run that changes an extension's behaviour also updates its docs in the same proposal group and keeps its change document's Status: line honest — wip when it claims ready work, completed when the work is done; only a person establishes draft or ready, and acceptance is what establishes any status. (BO_0201, BO_0254)
conventions.workVocabulary: Documents carry a decision vocabulary (BO_0244): a text block may have a kind, and reason-bearing relations connect blocks. Two rules, whichever tool writes them: a relation is proposed with a reason naming the condition that connects its ends — never that they seem related — and with origin inferred or derived, since a run never declares; and each end names a block by blockId, of this document or another, never a retired or discarded one, and never the same block twice. A relation anchored a claim until BO_0288; claim and asserts are calliopa-refine's vocabulary now and no kernel tool reads or writes them. Propose these through propose_document_changes (items kind, relate, reason, derive), never by statement, so review sees them as the editor would have written them.
conventions.writeShapeFollowsFrequency: Choose the write path by how often the operation happens, not by what it touches. Continuous editing stages candidates with no confirmation and one deliberate act to establish them; an occasional deliberate act — creating a channel, filing something into one — takes the confirmation directly, where the ceremony is proportionate. Both are the same architecture; only the frequency differs, and reaching for one shape everywhere makes typing intolerable or truth too cheap.

content.label: Extend

conventions.authoringRoutes: Two routes produce the same graph shape; pick one per change and never mix them. (1) Direct CCGW staging — what the examples below show: you write CREATE/SET and stage every partOf and dependsOn relation yourself. (2) The materializer round-trip — checkout into a working tree, edit files, commit — which derives partOf from the tree layout and dependsOn from the manifest dependencies map, so you never write a relation by hand. Route 2 is the default for human and agent authoring alike, and the kernel workspace tools ARE route 2 for a run: calliopa_workspace_checkout, _list, _read, _edit, _create, _delete, _build, _check, _test, _diff and _commit work a real tree on the kernel and stage its whole diff into your group. A Block that does not materialize (ext.skill, ext.settings, ext.migration, ext.blocktype, ext.relationtype, ext.intention) is reached by route 1, or carried by a members sidecar on kernel commit --members.
conventions.binaryAssets: Binary files travel: a binary in the diff becomes an ext.source Block whose code is a blob reference, the bytes uploaded through PUT /v1/blobs before the referencing mutation and hash-verified. The shell's favicon, PNGs and font ship this way.
conventions.breakingChanges: Tightening an established definition is gated; loosening it is free. Adding a required property, adding a unique property already duplicated, narrowing permitted children, enabling singleOpenCandidate, renaming, or removing a definition are breaking *when the type has established content* — and only then, so the same change is refused on a populated type and permitted on an empty one. A breaking change needs an ext.migration Block in the same group naming the types it covers, with a rationale and the operations that transform existing content travelling alongside; its authority is the human review of that group, not machinery. Removing a required property needs none, because requiring less invalidates nothing.
conventions.capabilities: The manifest capabilities object carries renders — the surface kinds the extension renders, as plural nouns: routes, views — and ccgwScopes, the CCGW operations its skills need, absent when the extension reads nothing. Nothing validates the shape, so a misspelled capabilities key builds clean and is never noticed.
conventions.checkWhereEnforcementRuns: A declaration is only enforced where something reads it. permittedChildTypes is honoured by the pages layer, and the pages layer is mounted in the production cell rather than the dogfood app — so in a dogfood deployment the declaration is real, resolved, and unenforced. Before relying on any declared constraint, find the code that acts on it and confirm that code is reachable from where the writes happen. When it is not, the surface owns the constraint and the gap belongs in the record.
conventions.codeRun: A run that changes an extension names the change document it works on, and everything follows from that: the run stages into that change's own proposal group rather than one minted for the run, so however many runs a change takes it arrives as ONE proposal for the person to answer; and the build tree belongs to that group, so a second run finds the first's tree with its dependencies already installed. The order: read the extension's docs/ and the change document the run names — the requirements live there, not in the command; calliopa_workspace_checkout; read and edit with the workspace tools; then calliopa_workspace_build, calliopa_workspace_check and calliopa_workspace_test until all three are green, because the person does not read your diff and the green gates plus your own account of what you did are most of what they judge the change by; then calliopa_workspace_commit with a rationale. Write the docs and the change document's Status: line in the SAME commit as the code: a proposal that changes behaviour and leaves the docs behind is incomplete and is not accepted as complete.
conventions.crossExtensionImports: The shell imports its extensions and an extension may import the shell's lib and server modules by the ~/ alias; the tree is one pnpm package, so every import resolves and builds. Nothing enforces the manifest's dependsOn against those imports — declare what you import anyway, because the dependency edge is what makes the relationship traversable in the graph.
conventions.declaredBaseline: On the direct CCGW route the mutation must carry dataRevision — the pin the change was computed against. An auto-created proposal group records it as its baseDataRevision, and acceptance conflict-checks against that base. Omit it and the group bases at 0, so acceptance refuses with mutation_resolution_failed conflicts with truth that moved past its base revision 0 — a refusal that names a conflict but is really a missing baseline, and that only appears at acceptance, long after staging looked successful. The materializer route passes the checkout pin for you, which is why this trap belongs to route 1 alone.
conventions.definitionShape: Definition fields are data, not prose. In an ext.blocktype or ext.relationtype Block, requiredProperties, uniqueProperties, permittedChildTypes and runProperties are lists of property-name strings; block and singleOpenCandidate are booleans. A string where a list belongs parses to nothing at all — uniqueProperties: "name among active channels" declares no unique property and the rule silently never fires, which is far worse than a refusal because the definition still reads correctly to a human. Put the qualifier in a separate descriptive field, never inside the declaration. The same rule governs the manifest: dependencies is a map of extension id to semver range, capabilities is an object, and category is exactly bundled or individual.
conventions.dependencyReferences: A dependency on another extension is a dependsOn relation from the depending manifest to the dependency manifest, with the semver range recorded in the depending manifest dependencies map keyed by extension id — the range is content because a relation stores no properties, and the relation is what makes the dependency traversable. On the materializer route kernel commit derives the edge from the map; on the direct route you stage it. A dependencies entry naming an extension with no manifest, established or added by the same change, is refused. Two extensions added together may depend on each other. The range is checked twice: the registry scan fails a build whose tree holds a version outside a declared range (dependency_out_of_range), and the kernel refuses a version flip or an activation that would serve one before writing it (BO_0219). A version is the manifest version label at the subtree's last established state under it: bump version when you want a state of the subtree to be a version a person can serve from the extension view; two revisions under one label are one version, its last state.
conventions.deploymentIsSeparate: Acceptance and deployment are two acts. Accepting a proposal establishes truth at a new dataRevision; the kernel keeps serving the promoted release pin until kernel pin --to head moves it, building the candidate before it promotes. An accepted extension is therefore not yet a running one, and nothing warns that the two have diverged — verify the surface appears rather than inferring it from acceptance.
conventions.derivedFiles: Files matching *.gen.* are build output, never content, and the commit path skips them. The tree root's node_modules/, dist/ and server/ are the build's derived directories and are never committed either; a nested src/server/ is ordinary source.
conventions.docs: An extension carries its owner's knowledge beside its code, as ext.source members under docs/: docs/system/<area>/<topic>.md under the live-line protocol — a list item's marker is its commitment (* fixed, - mutable), its checkbox its state ([ ] open, [x] claimed, none is truth), a line beginning 'Functional question' awaits the owner, and a task identifier (XX_0000_000) ties a line to the change that made it true. docs/system/system.md's Purpose section is what the extension is for; README.md is the fallback; the skill's goal is the last resort. An extension's changes are its own docs/changes/ members (BO_0254): docs/changes/<PREFIX>_NNNN_TYPE_<short-name>.md in its subtree, finished ones under docs/changes/completed/, each carrying its status in a Status: line from idea, draft, ready, wip, completed, rejected. They are written and revised the way every other docs member is — from a checkout, in the proposal that carries the code — and rendered read-only in the shell's Extensions section. A run working from a checkout writes them like any other member, in the proposal that carries the code — which is what the workspace tools are for. BO_0254 decided that a change document is not written through the DOCUMENT tools (create_document carries neither change nor status), not that a run holds no checkout. The shell renders the system docs as a navigable network for the owner, so a change to an extension is not complete until its docs say so: convert the [x] lines you claimed into truth, add [ ] follow-ups for what remains, keep the identifiers, and write the change document's Status: line in the same proposal. Read the docs before changing the code; they are where the requirements live. (BO_0201, BO_0254) An extension may be started from the shell's Extensions section with a manifest and a docs/system/system.md alone — its purpose under Purpose, version 0.1.0, individual, no entrypoint, nothing to serve (BO_0224); the first topic names the extension's prefix, and the first code arrives through this skill as a proposal. An extension can leave an instance as one file — the kernel's export: its tree — its change documents among it — and its members — and enter another as a proposal the owner accepts, arriving switched off; ext.settings, activation and pins never travel, and the archive's category lands as individual.
conventions.domainVocabulary: A domain vocabulary is ext.blocktype and ext.relationtype Blocks in an extension of its own, depending on ui.shell — never inside the shell, which stays domain-neutral. Neither Block materializes, so the definitions are staged through direct CCGW or a members sidecar while the extension's sources go through the materializer; that is one rung, two routes, and they must not be mixed inside a single change. Declare uniqueness with uniqueProperties and let the lifecycle carry the qualifier: declared uniqueness is scoped to established revisions, so retiring a node frees its unique values and a "retired" or "archived" flag kept in content does not, because a flagged node stays established and keeps claiming them.
conventions.draftingSurfacesReadThroughTheirDraft: A surface that stages before establishing has two halves, and the staged half is invisible by design. Staged content is a candidate and does not resolve at head, so every read in a drafting surface must carry the draft’s overlay — the list that finds unoffered drafts, and the read that shows what was just written. Getting this wrong does not produce an error: it produces a dead end, where the author is told to offer a draft they cannot see or reach. Verify that the author can see what they wrote, not only that the write succeeded.
conventions.featureExtensions: A feature extension carries code, not values. The first is settings: src/extensions/settings/ holds the view (settings.tsx), the server modules (server/connections.ts, server/connection-tests.ts, server/adapters.ts) and the feature's migrations (migrations/*.sql, one sequence with the shell's own migrations/ ordered by file name and applied by the tree's serve entry). The shell keeps the thin route files under src/routes/api/settings/ importing from ~/extensions/settings/server/…, and its manifest declares dependencies {"ui.shell": ">=0.1.0"}. Values the feature stores stay where the feature keeps them — the shell's encrypted connection store — never in ext.settings Blocks, which are plain graph content.
conventions.freshNamesAreForced: A graph definition may never shadow a code-registered type, so the frozen vocabulary’s names are unavailable: Page, Paragraph, Note and Document are all taken. Reincarnating a model therefore means fresh names carrying proven mechanics — which is the intended posture anyway, but the refusal enforces it whether or not you meant it.
conventions.migrations: The tree owns its schema. scripts/lib/migrations.mjs reads migrations/ and every src/extensions/<id>/migrations/ as one sequence ordered by file name, records each in schema_migrations, and the serve entry applies pending ones before it listens — except under the promotion gate's probe (CALLIOPA_SERVE_PROBE=1), which never migrates. Number a new migration after the highest existing one across both places.
conventions.naming: The manifest id is the extension id — lowercase letters and digits, starting with a letter, in parts joined by a dot or a hyphen, exactly ^[a-z][a-z0-9]*([.-][a-z0-9]+)*$, the rule the kernel's create enforces (BO_0224) — and must equal its directory name under src/extensions/ — the commit path refuses a mismatch. Source Blocks are <extId>.<path>. A contribution Block, if one is ever staged, carries a content id equal to its file name.
conventions.orderingLivesOnTheChild: Ordering is a content property on the child block, never on the containment relation, because a Relation stores no properties — a core-model fact, not a design choice. Use a base-36 fractional string compared as an ordinary string, so inserting between two siblings mints a key between theirs and writes one block instead of renumbering the set.
conventions.rulesTheGraphCannotExpress: Some settled rules have no home in the meta-schema and end up enforced in surfaces: which node types are ineligible as a relation’s endpoints, and permitted children wherever the enforcing layer is unreachable. Record each one where the rule is written rather than letting the surface be its only statement, because a rule living only in a surface is a rule the next surface will not know.
conventions.shellShape: The shell of this graph is calliopa-app, imported as ui.shell (BO_0200): a Qwik City application with file-convention routes under src/routes/ and compiled-in views (src/lib/views.ts), root-mapped as a whole. There is no runtime registry, no generated route map and no ext.uicontribution contract in this shell — the kernel still validates contribution Blocks on commit, but nothing reads them. An extension reaches the user through the shell's own source: the shell imports the extension's modules by path (~/extensions/<extId>/…) from a route file under src/routes/, a view entry in src/lib/views.ts, or a server module — so a new feature extension is one proposal that adds the subtree and the import lines in the shell, both root-mapped by the same kernel commit.
conventions.structuralVocabularies: A vocabulary with structure — containment, ordering, permitted children — is a different problem from a vocabulary of flat types. Reuse the code-registered CONTAINS relation rather than declaring a fresh containment type: the block machinery that enforces permitted children and nesting bounds resolves block types through the effective schema, so fresh graph-defined types inherit it, but every containment operation is written against CONTAINS. A fresh containment relation leaves permittedChildTypes declared and inert, which is the silent-no-op failure this system works hardest to avoid.
conventions.subtreeShape: One ext.manifest Block is the subtree root. Every member Block — ext.source, ext.blocktype, ext.relationtype, ext.skill, ext.uicontribution — carries a partOf relation to that manifest.
conventions.uiContributionContract: Retired with the calliopa-app shell. ext.uicontribution Blocks are still a valid member kind the kernel validates on commit (kind route, panel or command; content id equal to the file name), but this shell reads none of them; declare UI through the shell's own imports instead (shellShape).
conventions.wholeTreeCommits: The materializer diff is whole-tree: kernel commit stages everything that differs from the lockfile, not the subtree you were working in. Running the repository's own formatter while authoring an extension can therefore rewrite another extension's sources and stage them alongside your work — observed rewriting className to class across ui.shell. Check kernel status before every commit and confirm the file list is only yours; a foreign file in the list is a signal to stop, not a detail to accept.

content.goal: Create a new extension, or evolve an existing one, as a complete subtree of Blocks staged in exactly one atomic proposal through CCGW.
content.outputContract: Exactly one open proposal group staging the complete extension change — manifest, member Blocks, their partOf relations, and any dependsOn relations — with rationale and provenance. No writes outside the proposal, no established status, no partial subtree that could materialize half-applied. On the materializer route the same group is produced by kernel commit, with partOf and dependsOn derived rather than written by hand; the resulting graph shape is identical.
preconditions: The extension meta-schema definition Blocks are established truth; read the ext.blocktype and ext.relationtype definitions before staging.
The target extension id is decided and does not collide with an existing ext.manifest id.
Every extension named in the manifest dependencies map has a manifest, established or added by this same change.
The mutation context declares an agent identity scoped to one open proposal group; a skill execution never writes established truth.
The extension's docs/ members are read before its code is changed: docs/system/**/*.md carry the requirements and open work, and docs/changes/*.md the changes and the status each stands at (BO_0254).
For a code change: the change document the run names is read before the code is touched, and the run's group is that change's.

content.name: hasBlockRole
content.semantics: A block carries a block role: directed from any block in a document's reading order to the blockRole, at most one active per block, the roles extension's rule. Every block kind may carry one (BO_0299_Q8). Written as the person's own truth at once, never proposed. Declared by doc-block-roles under BO_0299_011.

content.name: hasDocumentRole
content.semantics: A document carries a document role: directed from the document to the documentRole, at most one active per document, the roles extension's rule, checked by a read before the write. Written as the person's own truth at once, never proposed (BO_0299_Q2, BO_0299_Q6). Declared by doc-block-roles under BO_0299_011.

content.name: offers
content.semantics: A document role offers a block role: directed from the documentRole to the blockRole, one document role per block role. Declared by doc-block-roles under BO_0299_011.

conventions.neverAssign: You never propose a document role or a block role: read_document_roles answers reads alone, and no item of propose_document_changes sets one. A block whose role is not offered by the current document role, or is retired, is still written by that role; say so in your conclusion if it matters.
conventions.profileSaysHow: A profile attached to the document may say how a role is written — its own blocks can carry the same roles. Where the profile speaks to a role, follow it; where it is silent, the role's description and its name are the guide.
conventions.readRolesFirst: Before proposing into a document, call read_document_roles once. The answer carries the document role, and per block in reading order its block role with its description — what a block of that role does, in the person's words.
conventions.roleIsNotTheTypographicRole: A block's blockRole is not its role in read_document: that one is the typographic role — paragraph, h1, quote. Keep the two apart.
conventions.writeByRole: A block's block role says what the block is for: write a Hook as a hook, a Closing as a closing that answers the hook. The role's description is the person's own account of it and outranks your idea of the word.

content.goal: Write a document that carries a document role by its roles: each block by the block role the person gave it, the whole by what the document role means, and never assign a role yourself.
content.outputContract: A conclusion naming the document role you wrote under and which block roles the proposed blocks serve; the blocks staged into the run's group; no role assigned or proposed.
content.permittedOperations: read_document_roles to read the document's role and each block's; propose_document_changes to propose the words. Nothing you hold assigns a role, and no item proposes one.
preconditions: read_document_roles answers for the document. If the document carries no document role, write it as you would any document and read nothing more here.
You can name the block you are writing into; its block role is read by blockId from the answer.

content.description: The document's role — a Story, an Essay — and each block's block role, in reading order, at your pin: what the person assigned, never a candidate's. Read it before proposing into a document that carries a document role, and write each block by its role: a Hook block is written as a hook. It stages nothing, and you never propose a role — assigning one is the person's act.

properties.formatCode: whether a settled edit of a code block, and an accepted one, is pretty-printed through the code service's formatter: absent or true means on, false means off; switched per document from the bar's Format code toggle, written by the person as their own edit (BO_0296_013)
properties.id: the document's identity, a UUID the shell mints; the node id is node:<id>
properties.intention: the marking a reader gave the whole document: the marks value of an established ext.intention declaration; unconstrained here because intention extensions are declared per instance and a permitted set in this declaration would refuse a marking the instance legitimately declares — the agent bridge refuses an unknown intention at run start
properties.lineNumbers: whether each line of a code block is numbered in the document: absent or true means shown, false means hidden; switched per document from the bar's Line numbers toggle, written by the person as their own edit, and nothing of it reaches a run (BO_0302_003)
properties.phase: the root's phase (BO_0249): proposed — a safe hypothetical environment, the default when absent; accepted — the wider system may rely on it; superseded — another root replaced it, named in supersededBy. The values are an established RootPhase declaration's, unconstrained here for the reason kind is (BO_0256_002)
properties.profile: the profile the reader attached to this document: the id of a document carrying record profile, whose established words the kernel supplies to a run started from a command in this document; absent means no profile; written as the person's own act by the profiles extension (BO_0298_010)
properties.record: the record slot carried over from the previous document type: names a record declaration; no permitted set, per the recorded non-enforcement of BO_0199_002
properties.runtime: the runtime the document is connected to for running its code blocks, by its id; absent means none. Written by the kernel as the person's own edit (BO_0289)
properties.supersededBy: the id of the root that superseded this one; present only with phase superseded, written in the same mutation that accepts the successor (BO_0249)
properties.title: the document's title
properties.venue: the venue a manuscript of this document is made for, a word the manuscripts extension knows — generic or ieee (BO_0293)

content.semantics: The one product-level document kind: a node with a title whose content is its ordered child blocks, held as CONTAINS relations from the document to each block rather than nested in its revision. A document is not itself a block: it is not ordered among siblings and nothing contains it. At most one open candidate per document. Declared by ui.shell under BO_0207_011; the previous gateway's TypeScript definition of the same type is retired with the gateway. Since BO_0254 an extension's changes are its own docs/changes/ members, not documents: a document is a document. Since BO_0249 a root carries a phase — proposed, accepted or superseded — and, superseded, names its successor in supersededBy.

content.semantics: A display equation: one block holding exact TeX, drawn typeset wherever it is read and never as its source. Declared by documents under BO_0290; an equation stays an equation whatever renders it. Inline mathematics is not this type but a run of a text block carrying math: true whose text is its TeX, and a reference to a numbered equation is a run carrying equationRef with the equation's identity and no text of its own — both tolerated by the core's run shape, which requires a text string and nothing else.

properties.alt: what the picture shows, in words: the block's accessible name, and what the editor draws while there are no bytes yet
properties.caption: words under it, optional; a number needs none (BO_0295)

content.semantics: A picture. A leaf block, containable through CONTAINS and ordered by its order key like every block. It carries no authored text and takes no text editor. The bytes live in Garage behind CCGW and are reached only through the blob reference, which is the sole identity and integrity carrier; mediaType, size, width, height and alt are advisory. The block type belongs to this extension rather than to whatever makes the bytes, so a picture stays a picture when a generator is switched off (BO_0273, user decision 2026-09-21).

Narrowed from keep, pin, resolved, discarded by BO_0272: pin is fixate under its own name, a resolved block reads as discarded and the old keep as the resting state, until the next write stores it

properties.runs: the formatted text as an ordered list of runs, each carrying text and its own marks and no offsets; the core canonicalizes runs on every write

content.rationale: BO_0272 narrows text.disposition from keep, pin, resolved, discarded, prompt to fixate, discarded, prompt: the standing scale becomes three states — discard, keep, fixate — where keep is the absence of a value (user decision, 2026-09-21). Nothing is lost. A block carrying pin reads as fixate, which is the same standing under its own name; one carrying resolved reads as discarded, the remaining state for a block its reader had set aside; one carrying the old keep reads as the resting state, which is what the word now means. The mapping is the kernel's StandingOf and the shell's RETIRED, so a reader and a run are told the same of one block, and the next write stores the new value. This instance carried no block with any disposition when the declaration was revised (90 text blocks, checked over CCGW on 2026-09-21), so no content operation travels with it here.

content.name: derivedFrom
content.semantics: A block was derived from another block: directed from the derived block to a block it rests on, staged by the run that drafts it, so system-maintained from two accepted blocks is a fact the graph holds and provenance reads. Declared by ui.shell under BO_0244_006.

content.name: focuses
content.semantics: A document is focused work on a block: directed from the child document to the text block it elaborates, at most one document per block, the shell's rule. The block keeps its place in its parent; deleting the child closes the edge. Declared by ui.shell under CA_0047_001.

content.name: retired
content.semantics: Records that a block left a document's reading order without being deleted, directed from the document to the block. Retiring a block closes its CONTAINS validity and creates this relation in the same mutation; restoring closes this relation and creates a new CONTAINS. Closing containment alone would strand the block beyond any rooted read, so retirement is recorded as its own relation and the retired list is an ordinary read from the document. Containment itself is the core's CONTAINS relation and needs no declaration here.

conventions.changeDocuments: An extension's changes are its own docs/changes/ members (BO_0254): docs/changes/<PREFIX>_NNNN_TYPE_<short-name>.md in its subtree, finished ones under docs/changes/completed/, each carrying its status in a Status: line from idea, draft, ready, wip, completed, rejected. They are written and revised the way every other docs member is — from a checkout, in the proposal that carries the code — and rendered read-only in the shell's Extensions section. A run working from the composer holds no checkout and so writes none. A document tool never writes one: create_document takes a title and a first block and nothing else. (BO_0254)
conventions.claimsAndRelations: A block asserts claims — its assertions in canonical words, each with an identity — and relations anchor on claims, never on blocks: a relate item names a source and a target claim by claimId, or a block by blockId with the claim's words to draft when the block asserts none; a block that asserts exactly one claim may be named alone. A relation is proposed with a reason naming the condition that connects its ends (cache reuse is safe only while the context is unchanged), never that they seem related, and with origin inferred or derived — a run never declares. A block's kind says what it is in the decision vocabulary (assumption, question, evidence, decision, …); a derive item says which blocks a block the same group inserts rests on. A relation ends by its state and is never removed. (BO_0244)
conventions.commit: A commit command is answered by a proposal, never by a write (BO_0249_012; material §46, rule 19): when the command says 'yes, this is the decision', 'treat this as the requirement', 'make this the accepted direction' or the like, stage exactly one phase item {kind: "phase", phase: "accepted"} on the document the command is about, with the rationale as one sentence of consequences drawn from the relations sourced on the document's claims and the judgements standing on its blocks — never a decision block, never a rewrite of the pinned synthesis. The shell draws that proposal as the transition card under the intent, and the reader's press on Establish is the one confirmation. This rule lives here because a person's run reads this skill whatever the document's intention; refine's conventions carry it as well. 'This' in a commit command is the document, never a block: a block the reader marked or referenced says where the decision is stated, so the phase item is the answer even then — mark that block's kind decision in the same proposal if it is not already, but a kind item alone answers nothing (found live 2026-09-15: two runs answered 'yes, this is the decision' with a marked block by a kind item and no phase). The rationale's one sentence of consequences also names the proposals standing unanswered in the document, since accepting the direction leaves them to be answered (BO_0271).
conventions.marks: A run carries text and, when it has any, marks among bold, italic, strikethrough and code, and may carry a link. Marks are not declared in the graph's vocabulary; the editor's set is the one that renders.
conventions.notes: A read and each proposed item may carry a note: one short line, at most 80 characters, saying what you do with the block. The person sees it on the block while you work, and on the proposal after. Give one when the plain words — Reading, Proposes a rewrite, Proposes removal — would not say what you are doing; leave it out otherwise. A note is never the change itself (BO_0265).
conventions.openProposals: The document you work in is not settled: other runs' proposals may stand unanswered on its blocks, and read_document answers them (BO_0271). Every block carries proposal — {group, item, proposer, kind, words, refinable, reason} — when another group has proposed against it, and the document carries proposedInserts, the new blocks proposed into it, each with where it would stand. Read them before writing anything new. What stands and needs sharpening is refined in place, never proposed again beside it: a block keeps one open proposal, so a second rewrite of the same block is refused by the core. A refinement is a replace carrying refines: {group, item} — the group and item read_document answered — with the runs and, if it changes, the role; it lands on that proposal's candidate, under that group, and the person answers once. A proposed insert is refined the same way, by its group and item. Stage only what needs changing. Where a standing proposal already says what you would say, leave its words as they are; say that you left it plainly only when there is really nothing to add anywhere. The document's own blocks — accepted text — are left as they are unless the command referenced one (a marked block or passage) or plainly asks for those words to change; every proposal the person has not answered is open matter, accepted words are not. A proposal whose refinable is false is context: read it, build on what it says, never propose against it — its reason says why: a run still going may restage the same block a moment later, another person's branch is theirs, a candidate the system derived is answered by the person alone, a fixated framing is kept, an answered member is settled, and a removal or a move has no words to refine. Your final words say what you refined and whose it was, and what you left standing because it already said it. When the command asks to reconcile, merge or reduce the standing proposals (BO_0286): refine the proposals that stay, so the reconciled words live in them; withdraw the ones those words make surplus with a withdraw item — proposal: {group, item}, successor: the standing item or the index of the item in this call that supersedes it, withdrawalReason: one short line where the successor does not say it — and stage nothing beside them. A withdrawal is a proposal, never an answer: the item stays open with its words, the person rejects it with one press or accepts it anyway, and accepting the successor rejects what it supersedes in the same press. Any withdrawable item may be withdrawn, a removal or a move too, which then leaves the block as it stands. The final words say how many proposals were refined and how many withdrawn, and in whose favour.
conventions.prompts: A block with the prompt standing is a command the reader wrote in the document and sent, not material of it (BO_0267): never rewrite, remove or move it, and do not build on it unless the command asks. When your run was sent from a block, the instructions name it. Every command given in a document is answered by proposing into it: when the command asks a question, the answer is staged directly after the block the command was sent from, as the blocks the reader should read it as (conventions.structure), and your final words say what you staged.
conventions.readerAnswersPerItem: Each item is decided on its own in the editor. Keep an item to one intent, so a reader can accept the heading and reject the rewrite.
conventions.structure: What you stage arrives as the structure you wrote, never as one block holding all of it (BO_0270). Split the content at its headings: a heading is its own text block with the role it has — h1, h2, h3 — and a block's runs never carry # characters, which nothing renders. Under a heading each paragraph is its own block, and each list item is its own block with its marker as plain text, since no role renders a list; a fenced code block stays one text block, because it is one unit; and a table is a table block — kind table, with its typed columns (text, number, date, boolean) and its rows, one block whole (BO_0287) — never pipes in a paragraph. An equation is an equation block — kind equation, carrying the exact TeX it is set from, optionally a caption and numbered when its author asks for a number (BO_0290) — never TeX in a paragraph; mathematics inside a sentence is a run of that sentence carrying math: true whose text is its TeX, and a reference to a numbered equation is a run carrying equationRef with that equation's identity and no text of its own. A picture carries an optional caption and numbered when its author asks for a figure number, and a table numbered likewise (BO_0295); A code block carries an optional caption and numbered when its author asks for a listing number, counted apart from figures and tables (BO_0303); read_document answers a numbered code block's number, and a reference to it reads Listing N; a reference to a numbered figure — a picture, or an output a person numbered — is a run carrying figureRef with its identity and no text of its own, and to a numbered table a run carrying tableRef. A reference to any block of the document — a section by its heading, a paragraph, or a numbered figure, table or equation — is a run of its sentence carrying blockRef with that block's identity and no text of its own (BO_0300); read_document answers each as its label — Figure 3, Table 1, (2), the heading's words, or Remark N for a paragraph another sentence refers to, which the manuscript then sets apart as a numbered remark — or missing when the block is outside the reading order; prefer blockRef over figureRef, tableRef and equationRef, which remain read for the sentences that carry them. A citation is a run of its sentence carrying cite — {work, locator?}: the identity of a work of the instance's bibliography, and where in it when the claim rests on one place, such as p. 12 — whose text is empty, never a bracketed number or an author and year typed into the words (BO_0291); read_document answers each citation's number, or missing when its work is gone, and how the reader sees it drawn is the document's citation style. Never set a caption or numbered on an output: an output is what an execution produced, and its caption and number are the person's. A number is never written: read_document answers the number the document's order gives each numbered equation, figure, table and listing — each kind counted apart — and a reference answers the number it resolves to, or missing when its block is gone or asks for none. A change to a table is a replace of that one block carrying the whole table; where a file stands behind it, read_document says so with its row count and the rows you read are its first hundred, and your replace drops the file, since the cells you propose are the whole table. A paper's abstract is one text block with the role abstract, wherever it stands; a manuscript's authors, affiliations, keywords and venue are the document's own properties, set by a person, and a run proposes none of them (BO_0293). Never invent structure: content that carries no heading is given none, and a one-sentence answer is one block by this rule rather than by an exception. A rewrite carries it too: rewriting a block into content with headings stages the replace beside the inserts in the one group, with the rationale saying the items are one change.

examples.readTheBlocksYouWorkOn: read_document {documentId} → read_blocks {documentId, blockIds: [blockId, blockId], note: 'Checking the definition against its use'} → propose_document_changes {documentId, rationale, items: [{kind: replace, blockId, runs: [{text: '...'}], note: 'Tightens the definition'}]}
examples.reconcileStandingProposals: read_document {documentId} → twenty proposed inserts stand from an ended run, all refinable → read_blocks {documentId, blockIds: […]} → propose_document_changes {documentId, rationale: 'Reconciles the twenty proposed blocks into one argument of six: the six that carry it are refined, the fourteen they absorb are withdrawn in their favour', items: [{kind: replace, refines: {group: 'node:run-…', item: 'node:run-…|insert|node:<a>'}, runs: […]}, …, {kind: withdraw, proposal: {group: 'node:run-…', item: 'node:run-…|insert|node:<b>'}, successor: {index: 0}, withdrawalReason: 'folded into the opening paragraph'}, …]} — nothing is staged beside the standing proposals; the person answers each withdrawn block from its chip, or all of them by accepting the refined ones
examples.refineAStandingProposal: read_document {documentId} → the block carries proposal {group: 'node:run-…', item: 'node:run-…|replace|node:<blockId>', proposer: 'Codex', kind: 'rewrite', words: '…', refinable: true} → read_blocks {documentId, blockIds: [blockId]} → propose_document_changes {documentId, rationale: 'Sharpens the standing rewrite of the definition: the words are Codex's with the exception stated', items: [{kind: replace, refines: {group: 'node:run-…', item: 'node:run-…|replace|node:<blockId>'}, runs: [{text: '…'}], note: 'Sharpens the standing rewrite'}]} — the block still carries one proposal, now with these words, and the person answers once
examples.relateTwoClaims: read_document {documentId} → find the claims → propose_document_changes {documentId, rationale, items: [{kind: relate, relation: {kind: dependsOn, reason: [{text: 'the cache is safe only while the request sees one revision'}], origin: inferred, source: {claimId}, target: {blockId, claim: [{text: 'A request sees one stable revision.'}]}}}]}
examples.reviseAReason: propose_document_changes {documentId, rationale, items: [{kind: reason, relationId, reason: [{text: '...'}]}]}
examples.rewriteAParagraph: read_document {documentId} → find the block whose runs carry the sentence → read_blocks {documentId, blockIds: [blockId]} → propose_document_changes {documentId, rationale, items: [{kind: replace, blockId, runs: [{text: '...'}]}]}
examples.rewriteIntoSections: a rewrite that grows sections keeps the block and adds the rest in the same group: propose_document_changes {documentId, rationale: 'One change: the paragraph becomes two sections.', items: [{kind: replace, blockId, runs: [{text: 'The opening, rewritten.'}]}, {kind: insert, block: {kind: text, role: h3, runs: [{text: 'Trade-offs'}]}, placement: {after: blockId}}, {kind: insert, block: {kind: text, runs: [{text: 'What they are.'}]}, placement: {after: blockId}}]}
examples.sayWhatABlockRestsOn: propose_document_changes {documentId, rationale, items: [{kind: insert, block: {...}, placement}, {kind: derive, blockId: <the inserted block>, from: [blockId, blockId]}]}
examples.setAKind: propose_document_changes {documentId, rationale, items: [{kind: kind, blockId, blockKind: assumption}]}

content.goal: Read and propose changes to the documents a reader writes in, through the kernel toolset's document tools, so a run's proposal lands exactly what the editor would have written and is reviewed per item.
content.outputContract: One propose_document_changes call per coherent change to one document, with a rationale saying why. Report the group the tool answered and what it stages; never claim the change is accepted. A refusal envelope is an answer: read its diagnostics and adjust the items rather than retrying the same call. A commit command — 'yes, this is the decision', 'treat this as the requirement', 'make this the accepted direction' — is answered by one phase item {kind: "phase", phase: "accepted"} on the document, whatever block is marked or referenced: the marks say where the decision is stated, not what to change, and a kind item alone is the wrong answer (conventions.commit). A commit's sentence of consequences names the proposals standing unanswered in the document. A refinement is reported as what it refined and whose proposal that was; a standing proposal left as it stands because it already says it is reported as left, not as done (conventions.openProposals). A reconciliation is reported as how many standing proposals were refined and how many withdrawn, and in whose favour, never as new blocks staged beside them.
content.permittedOperations: list_documents to find a document by title, and an extension's changes by change — each row carries change and status for a change document; read_document for its blocks in reading order with their identities, kinds, roles and runs, and for a change document its extension and status; read_blocks for only the blocks it names, in reading order and in read_document's shape, which is how the person sees what you look at (BO_0265); propose_document_changes with items of kind replace (runs and/or role for a block), insert (a new text or divider block at a placement), remove (a block leaves the reading order, retired rather than deleted), move (a block to a placement) and status (a change document's status, one of idea, draft, ready, wip, completed, rejected); create_document for a new document with a title, its first block and — for a change of an extension — change naming the extension and a status, idea unless said. Everything stages into this run's proposal group; nothing writes truth. The statement tools remain available for anything beyond documents. — and, since BO_0244, kind (a block's blockKind, none clears it), claim (add a claim to a block, or revise one by claimId), relate (a reason-bearing relation between two claims), reason (a relation's new reason) and derive (the blocks a block rests on). read_document answers each block's blockKind, claims, provenance and derivedFrom, and the document's relations with both ends. Since BO_0249, phase: the root's phase — {kind: "phase", phase: proposed | accepted | superseded, supersededBy only with superseded} on the document itself, refused on a change document, whose status is its lifecycle. An agent proposes a phase and never sets it; the reader establishes it from the transition card. Since BO_0271, read_document and read_blocks answer on each block its proposal — the standing proposal another group holds against it: group, item, proposer, kind (rewrite, removal, move), words, refinable and, when not refinable, reason — and the document's proposedInserts, each with its placement; and a replace item may carry refines: {group, item}, landing its runs and role on that proposal's candidate in that group instead of in this run's, which is how a standing proposal is refined (conventions.openProposals). Since BO_0286, withdraw: {kind: "withdraw", proposal: {group, item}, successor?: {group, item} | {index}, withdrawalReason?} marks a standing proposal as surplus, on the proposal itself, for the person to reject with one press; read_document answers each standing proposal's withdrawable and, when a run has proposed one, its withdrawnBy — the run, its agent, the successor and the reason (conventions.openProposals).
content.preconditions: The run holds the kernel toolset. The document to change exists at the run's pin; read it once with read_document to find your way, then read the blocks you work on with read_blocks before proposing against them — the person sees each block you read marked while you read it — because a replace or a move names a block by the identity those reads answered.

conventions.mentionsAreDerived: A mention is resolved from the words when the document is read and stored nowhere: you write the words, and the connection follows. Do not add links, marks or brackets to make one.
conventions.neverMark: You never mark a document as a keyword, give it or its blocks a role, or propose a definition into a keyword's document unless asked to in that document: marking and defining are the person's acts.
conventions.preferTheTitle: Use the keyword's title in your words rather than an alias, so the mention is drawn and the glossary carries the name the person chose. A plural or a possessive of the title is fine; a different word is not the keyword.
conventions.readKeywordsFirst: Before proposing into a document, call read_keywords once. Where the document mentions a keyword, its definition is in the answer; where you are about to write a keyword the document does not mention yet, the instance's keywords are listed by name.
conventions.writeByTheDefinition: Write about a keyword as its definition has it. The definition is the person's own account and outranks your idea of the word; where it is silent, the keyword's document is the next place to read.

content.goal: Write about a keyword as the keyword's own document defines it: read the definition before writing, keep the keyword's title, and never mark a document as a keyword yourself.
content.outputContract: A conclusion naming the keywords the proposed words are about and where their definitions were read; the blocks staged into the run's group; no keyword marked and no role assigned.
content.permittedOperations: read_keywords to read the document's mentions and the instance's keywords; read_document to read a keyword's document whole when its definition is not enough; propose_document_changes to propose the words. Nothing you hold marks a keyword or assigns a role.
preconditions: read_keywords answers for the document. If the instance holds no keywords, write as you would any document and read nothing more here.
A keyword is a document the person gave the keyword role; its definition and its aliases are blocks of that document under roles the person named.

content.description: The keywords this document mentions, in reading order at your pin — each mention's block and character range, the keyword's title, its definition and its aliases — and the names of every keyword the instance holds. Read it before writing about a keyword, and write it as its definition has it. It stages nothing, and you never mark a document as a keyword or give it a role — that is the person's act.

document.description: The document, as a record id.

content.name: read_keywords
manuscript

properties.by: who made it: a person's name, or the run that made it
properties.files: the LaTeX source, its .bib and the PDF, each the core's blob reference with its filename, hoisted to a top-level list
properties.id: the manuscript's identity, a UUID; the node id is node:<id>
properties.log: the typesetting's errors and warnings, in order
properties.of: the document the manuscript was made of
properties.omitted: what the projection left out and why, in words
properties.outcome: what the typesetting answered: ok, errors, failed or timed out
properties.title: the document's title at the revision projected
properties.venue: the venue it was made for

content.semantics: A manuscript made of a document and kept (BO_0293): a root node with no parent and no block flag, as a work is, so it is never offered among the kinds a document's block may take.

conventions.aFileNotABlock: A run's manuscript is a file of the document: it proposes no block and changes no property. Do not describe it as a change to the document.
conventions.onceIsEnough: Every manuscript made is kept on the document and listed with your process. Make one, read it, and say what you found; make another only after the document changed.
conventions.readBeforeMaking: Read the document first. A manuscript with no abstract, no authors or no numbered figure is what the document has, not a fault of the tool: propose the missing block or say what front matter the person has to set, rather than making manuscript after manuscript.
conventions.readTheAnswer: The answer is the LaTeX source, the log's warnings and what was left out — never the PDF. Read the omitted list first: every line names a block the paper could not carry and why. Then the warnings. Then the source, for what the venue's rules ask that the document does not give.
conventions.sayItInTheDocument: What the manuscript needs goes into the document as a proposal — a question block under the section it concerns, or the missing block itself — and into your conclusion. Never edit the source: the manuscript is a projection of the record, and the record is what is corrected.

content.goal: Make a manuscript of the document you work in when the person asks for one, or when the document is to be submitted and a reading of it against the venue's rules is wanted; read what came back and say in the document what the manuscript needs.
content.outputContract: A conclusion naming the venue, the outcome, what was left out and what the document needs for the venue; the kept manuscript staged into the run's group with its files; any proposed blocks staged beside it.
content.permittedOperations: make_manuscript, the kernel's, to make and keep a manuscript of a document at your pin for a venue: generic or ieee, else the document's own venue, else generic. read_document to read the front matter and the blocks first. propose_document_changes to say in the document what the manuscript needs. Nothing you hold writes truth.
preconditions: The manuscripts extension is active and the instance has a typesetting service: make_manuscript is listed, and refuses in words when there is no service.

The document holds what a manuscript is made of at your pin: a title, its front matter, an abstract block, sections, numbered figures and tables, citations from the bibliography. What is not there is not in the manuscript — nothing is typed a second time.

conventions.oneAtATime: Propose one picture per place it is wanted. A run that stages six pictures has decided six times that someone should pay.
conventions.quoteBeforeProposing: Ask what it would cost first, and put the figure in your answer, so the person decides with the price in front of them.
conventions.theBlockIsThePrompt: Propose a picture from what the document already says. Leave `prompt` out unless the block's words would make a poor picture, and say why you replaced them.
conventions.theModelDecidesTheKind: A model makes pictures or moving pictures, not both. Name the model and let its kind follow; never ask for a kind the model does not make.

content.goal: Offer a picture where a document would be clearer for one, and never make it yourself. You propose; a person decides and pays.
content.outputContract: A conclusion naming what you proposed, which block it follows, and what it would cost; zero or more pending picture blocks staged into the run's group; and nothing made.
content.permittedOperations: quote_generation to say what something would cost, and propose_generation to stage a picture that is not made yet. Nothing you hold can spend: the press that bills is a person's, on a route no run can reach.
preconditions: A generator is signed in. If none is, say so and stop: the person signs in to Higgsfield or OpenArt in Settings, with their own subscription.
You can name the block the picture belongs after. A picture is made from a block's own words, so the block is the prompt.
The person has not said they do not want one. An unasked-for picture that costs money is worse than no picture.

content.description: Propose a picture or a moving picture after a block, made from that block's own words. It proposes and does not make: what you stage is a picture that does not exist yet, and a person presses to make it with the cost in front of them. You cannot spend, and no tool you hold can. Use it when a document would be clearer with a picture and you can say which block it belongs after.

afterBlockId.description: The block the picture follows, and whose words are its prompt.

documentId.description: The document, as a record id.

kind.description: image or video, matching the model's own kind.

model.description: The model, as the generators list them. The model decides whether a picture or a moving picture is made.

prompt.description: Words to use instead of the block's own. Leave it out unless the block's words would make a poor picture.

service.description: The generator: higgsfield or openart. Ask the person which they have signed in to rather than guessing.

content.name: propose_generation

content.description: What a picture or a moving picture would cost, before anyone makes it. Free: nothing is spent by asking. Use it when a person wonders whether something is worth making, or before you propose one, so the cost is in front of them when they decide.

kind.description: image or video, matching the model's own kind.

model.description: The model, as the generators list them. The model decides whether a picture or a moving picture is made.

prompt.description: The words the picture would be made from.

service.description: The generator: higgsfield or openart. Ask the person which they have signed in to rather than guessing.

content.name: quote_generation
assignment

properties.channel: the channel that takes the shape
properties.container: the container the site declares that the shape is taken into
properties.id: the assignment's identity, a UUID the extension mints; the node id is node:<id>
properties.parts: the list of {part, slot}: each of the shape's parts and the slot of that container it is assigned to

content.semantics: What a channel takes: one shape into one container the site declares, its parts assigned to slots. One per channel and shape, related to the channel by `takes` and to the shape by `of`; what it names is what the index read keeps when the site stops listing a key. PU_0003_001

content.name: binding

properties.address: the record's address at the channel: the slug a route names, freely editable until the record was ever published there and a permanent citation target afterwards
properties.channel: the channel; one binding per record and channel is the extension's rule, checked by a read before the write
properties.disclosure: the synthetic-media disclosure the channel's control needs
properties.fields: the values of the container's fields the site declares, typed as the index declares them
properties.id: the binding's identity, a UUID the extension mints; the node id is node:<id>
properties.number: the record's number at the channel, for a numbered container; typed by the author
properties.recordId: the deliverable or item this binding is about

content.semantics: What one record is worth at one channel, as authored. Observed facts — when it was published, its state — are never stored here; they are the log's. PU_0003_001

content.name: channel

properties.id: the channel's identity, a UUID the extension mints; the node id is node:<id>
properties.kind: the id of the channel kind this channel is of — an adapter the publishing extension ships; the registry in code is the roster, so the value is unconstrained here
properties.title: the channel's title, the author's own words for where this goes

content.semantics: A destination the author's work goes to, created by the author from the Channels category: a kind and a title. Its credential and configuration are a party record in the kernel's secret store under publishing-<id>, never in the graph, and its state is read from that record. It declares a contentIndex through `declares` when its kind reads an index from the destination. PU_0001_002

content.name: contentIndex

properties.channel: the channel that declared it; one index per channel is the extension's rule, checked by a read before the write
properties.containers: the containers the site declared, each with whether the last read still listed it
properties.copy: the site-wide copy fields the site declared, each with whether the last read still listed it
properties.id: the index's identity, a UUID the extension mints; the node id is node:<id>
properties.readAt: when the site was last read, as an ISO-8601 timestamp the extension stamps at the write
properties.slots: the slots the site declared, each with whether the last read still listed it

content.semantics: What a website declared at GET <address>/index, as the publishing extension stored it: containers with route templates and fields, slots typed by content class with their constraints, copy fields. A key the site no longer lists is kept and marked while something is assigned to it, dropped otherwise. PU_0001_002 PU_0001_007

content.name: deliverable

properties.id: the deliverable's identity, a UUID the extension mints; the node id is node:<id>
properties.title: the deliverable's title

content.semantics: An instance of a shape (`shaped`), gathering the items and nested deliverables that fill its parts (`gathers`). Nothing on it says where it went; that is the publication log's. PU_0002_001

content.name: export

properties.bytes: the blob reference: _kind blob, hash sha256:<objectId>, mediaType, size and the filename it arrived as
properties.id: the export's identity, a UUID the extension mints; the node id is node:<id>
properties.mediaType: the media type read off the file, restated beside the reference
properties.provenance: how it came to exist: ingested from outside, or produced here
properties.size: the size in bytes, restated beside the reference
properties.width: the export's width in pixels; its aspect is derived from the dimensions on the way out

content.semantics: One rendition of an item: content-addressed bytes in the graph's blob store, permanent once referenced. Replacing an export closes the item's `exported` relation to the old one and keeps it. PU_0002_001

content.name: item

properties.alt: the alt text of a picture
properties.durationSeconds: a video's or an audio's duration, read off the file
properties.height: a picture's height in pixels, read off the file
properties.id: the item's identity, a UUID the extension mints; the node id is node:<id>
properties.label: a short line naming the item, the author's
properties.synthetic: whether the item is synthetic media; stated per item, never defaulted, so a destination applies its own disclosure from it
properties.transcript: the words a video or an audio says, so an agent that cannot watch can read
properties.width: a picture's width in pixels, read off the file

content.semantics: One piece of content: its class, its machine facts, a label and its disclosure; its exports through `exported`, or its body document through `prose`. It may be gathered by several deliverables or by none; one gathered by none is standing. PU_0002_001

content.name: part

properties.cardinality: how many fill it: exactly one, at most one, one or more, any number
properties.class: the content class the items filling it are of, or `shape` for a part that nests another shape
properties.constraints: what the author requires of the items filling it at production time: aspect, maxDurationSeconds, minWidth, minHeight, formats
properties.id: the part's identity, a UUID the extension mints; the node id is node:<id>
properties.order: the part's place among its shape's parts: a fractional key compared as a string
properties.role: a label for what the author makes the part as
properties.shape: the shape a part of class shape nests
properties.title: the part's title

content.semantics: One part of a shape: a content class with a cardinality, a role and constraints, or a nested shape. Items fill it through `fills`. PU_0002_001

content.name: release

properties.act: publishing puts what the channel did not hold; retiring ends what it did
properties.at: when, as an ISO-8601 timestamp the extension stamps at the write
properties.detail: what went wrong, on a failure; never carries a presented secret
properties.externalAddress: where the channel serves it, on a success
properties.externalId: the channel's own id for what it now holds, on a success
properties.id: the entry's identity, a UUID the extension mints; the node id is node:<id>
properties.objectIds: every content-addressed object the attempt sent, which are permanent once named here
properties.recordId: the record the attempt was about
properties.recordTitle: the record's title at the time, so the log reads without the record

content.semantics: One entry of the append-only publication log: created as an established revision and never revised, retired or removed. A record's state at a channel is derived from its entries. PU_0003_001

content.name: shape

properties.id: the shape's identity, a UUID the extension mints; the node id is node:<id>
properties.title: the shape's title, the author's word for the kind of deliverable it describes

content.semantics: A deliverable type the author defines — Episode, Statement, Weekly edition — composed of parts through `composes`, and nesting other shapes through `nests`. Which shapes exist is data; the concept is the publishing extension's. PU_0002_001

content.name: composes
content.semantics: A part of a shape. Directed shape to part.

content.name: declares
content.semantics: The index a channel declared. Directed channel to contentIndex; at most one active per channel.

content.name: exported
content.semantics: An export an item still exports. Directed item to export; closed when the export is replaced, the export kept.

content.name: fills
content.semantics: The part an item or a nested deliverable fills. Directed item or deliverable to part.

content.name: gathers
content.semantics: What a deliverable holds: an item, or a deliverable of a nested shape. Directed deliverable to item or deliverable; an item may be gathered by any number of deliverables.

content.name: nests
content.semantics: A shape a part of another shape nests. Directed outer shape to inner shape; never a cycle.

content.name: of
content.semantics: The shape an assignment takes. Directed assignment to shape.

content.name: prose
content.semantics: The body document of a prose item, in the shell's block model. Directed item to document; at most one active per item.

content.name: shaped
content.semantics: The shape a deliverable is an instance of. Directed deliverable to shape; exactly one active per deliverable.

content.name: takes
content.semantics: An assignment of a channel. Directed channel to assignment.

content.name: policy

properties.id: the policy's identity; the node id is node:<id>
properties.rule: who may establish a root under this policy: owner — the instance's owner and any human account the instance admits, the one rule today (BO_0249_006); named approvers, required reviewers and majorities are each their own change

content.semantics: An acceptance policy a root references through an acceptedBy relation (material §27): acceptance policy belongs to the block, never to the route, and a child inherits policy only through an explicit relation. Declared by ui.shell under BO_0249_006 with one permitted rule, owner, so the hook is the relation the material asks for and not a policy engine. It moved to relations with the root's phase under BO_0288_015, because what accepting a root would change is a relation traversal.

content.name: relation

properties.id: the relation's identity, a UUID the shell mints; the node id is node:<id>
properties.kind: what the source claim does to the target claim, from the material's list; derives-from is the derivedFrom provenance edge, not a kind here
properties.origin: declared by a person or a governed process; derived mechanically from accepted structure; inferred by a run — an inferred relation is a proposal until a person confirms it and never propagates pressure before
properties.reason: why the source matters to the target, as runs, in the reader's or the run's words: the condition that connects them, which is what makes propagation precise
properties.state: the relation's lifecycle: absent means declared; exercised once evaluated against a change; needsReview when its reason may no longer apply; orphaned when an end is gone; retired when intentionally ended. A relation ends by this state and is never RETIREd, so its record stays readable

content.semantics: A reason-bearing relation between two blocks: a node, because a Relation stores no properties and the reason is what carries consequence (data-model.md BO_0029_003). Joined to its ends by source and target edges leaving this node, so staging one revises neither end. Proposed is the node being a candidate, not a state. Declared by ui.shell under BO_0244_006, anchored on claims until BO_0288_015 moved it to relations and gave it the block: any block says something, and a claim only ever existed where refinement had been.

content.name: acceptedBy
content.semantics: A root's acceptance policy: directed from a document to the policy node whose rule says who may establish it. Absent, the root is under the owner rule. Declared by ui.shell under BO_0249_006, moved to relations with the phase under BO_0288_015.

content.name: source
content.semantics: A relation node's source block, the one whose change may matter; directed relation to text block. Declared by ui.shell under BO_0244_006, re-pointed from a claim by BO_0288_015.

content.name: target
content.semantics: A relation node's target block, the one that may be affected; directed relation to text block. Declared by ui.shell under BO_0244_006, re-pointed from a claim by BO_0288_015.

content.name: attachment

properties.file: a blob reference to the file's bytes; writing the node references them, so the blob store keeps them past the staging TTL
properties.filename: the file's name as the person attached it
properties.id: the attachment's identity, a UUID the shell mints when the command is sent; the node id is node:<id>
properties.mediaType: the file's media type: the browser's when it named one, else sniffed from its first bytes, else its extension's
properties.size: the file's size in bytes, at most 10 MB
properties.text: a blob reference to the text extracted from a PDF or Office document; absent for a file that is its own text and for any file with none
properties.textStatus: what a run can read of the file: text, extracted, empty (a PDF with no text layer or an Office file with no text), image, or none

content.semantics: The record of a file a person sent with a command: written as that person when the command is sent, one node per file, and named by the run it was sent with. It is the frame's, not a document's: nothing contains it and it contains nothing. Declared by ui.shell under BO_0229_007.
